name: work-decide
description: 'Takes the owner through the decisions his work items wait on, each with a recommendation, and records his answers. Use when he asks "what do you need from me", answers a waiting decision ("go with option B"), or states a project-wide decision. Not for a bare "yes" when this chat asked no question.'

# Work decide

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Shared rules: the work plugin's `references/conventions.md`, two folders above this skill's folder (`../../references/conventions.md`). To open another skill, Claude Code uses the Skill tool; Codex reads that skill's `SKILL.md`. Run each `toolkit` command alone, on its own line, in both hosts: never joined by `&&`, `;`, or a pipe, and never from a script (in Codex that runs it inside the sandbox, where it fails). Text (conventions, "Text in a command"): one-line values (`--note`, `--effect`, `--append-row`, `--title`) go in single quotes, with an apostrophe written `'\''`, because double quotes run backticks and `$(...)`; section and design text goes on standard input in Claude Code (`<file>` is `-`, followed by a quoted heredoc, `<<'EOF'`), and in Codex in `--text '<text>'` or a file in a new `mktemp -d` folder, deleted right after the command. Never change a record with a script. Ask the owner in the reply text, never through a question tool. No remote (`git remote` prints nothing): never run `git fetch`, and never report a fetch refusal as a blocker.

## Steps

1. Build the queue: requirements waiting for approval, designs marked proposed, items at stage 11 waiting for result approval, Open Questions rows where the owner decides, and memory proposals (records saved as `needs-review` because the owner did not answer "Save to memory?"). The command lists each decision once. Its "Agent to-do" lines are the agent's own steps, not decisions waiting on the owner: count and show only the decisions. A delivery offer, as an agent to-do or as an open question, belongs to `work-delegate`, the only skill that makes or records it: open it after the owner's other decisions.
   `toolkit work decisions`
2. The owner gave an answer without being asked ("approved", "go with B"): match it to exactly one waiting decision. If two could match, ask which one, naming both. A bare "yes", "ok", or "looks good" is not such an answer ("What counts as an answer").
3. Otherwise take the decisions one at a time, the one blocking the most work first. For each: what is being decided, the choices, your recommendation and its main reason, and what happens after each answer. Every decision carries a recommendation, even when it is the only one in the queue; a bare question is not enough. One decision per message, asked in the reply text.
4. A requirements approval: save his words as a history note first, so no later session asks him again. Then check the Agreed goal and the open questions. The goal still holds the template text: write the goal he was shown with the approval question, then record the approval. A requirement still has an open question linked: say which one, open `work-requirements` for it, and record the approval, without asking him again, once it is answered.
   `toolkit work show <id> --section Requirements`
   `toolkit work history <id> --note 'Owner'\''s words: <quote>' --effect 'Requirements approval to record.'`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Agreed goal" --text '<goal he was shown>'`
5. Record each answer where it belongs. Approvals (for requirements, first set each approved `R-xx` Status to Finalized and put who approved it and when in its Decision record, as `work-requirements` step 8 does; after it, a `build` or `data-load` item goes to `solution-design` unless the owner agreed to skip the design, and a skip is said in the final reply). The approve command marks the Open Questions rows that asked for that approval Answered and prints "Marked Q-xx Answered"; read that line, and do not mark those rows again by hand. An Open Questions answer: rewrite that row with the answer, the date, and status Answered (the delivery offer row: open `work-delegate`, which records it).
   `toolkit work approve <id> --requirements --by <owner>`
   `toolkit work approve <id> --design --by <owner>`
   `toolkit work approve <id> --result --by <owner>`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Open Questions" --set-file <file>`
   Then, for an approval or an answer: `waiting_on` set to `agent` when the agent continues (the approve command sets it to `none` by itself), unless another question for him on that item is still open; then one history note in the owner's words, with an `--effect` that says what the answer changes (a requirements approval has its note from step 4).
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`
   `toolkit work history <id> --note 'Owner'\''s words: <quote>' --effect '<what the answer changes>'`
6. A memory proposal: show its one line and whether you recommend keeping it. The agent does not rely on it until he approves it. Yes: approve it, and it becomes a current memory. No: reject it (the proposal is deleted), and never propose the same fact again under other words.
   `toolkit memory approve <key> --by <owner>`
   `toolkit memory reject <key>`
7. A decision for the whole project: add a `DECISIONS.md` row and save it with `publish-docs`. Run the command inside the worktree `publish-docs` opens, then let it commit (and push, when the project has a remote).
   `toolkit decision add --decision '<decision>' --why '<why>' --by <owner>`
8. A "no" or a change: record it as the answer, move the item back (for example to refinement), and open the skill that redoes the work.
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 02-refinement`
9. Lead with "Not saved" if any write failed. When an answer changed an item's next step, update the current focus (`../../references/conventions.md`, "The current focus"). When the queue is empty, say so and offer to continue unblocked items with `work-on`. End the reply with the next decision's question, or the exact words that continue.

## What counts as an answer

- Only the owner's explicit words count. Quote them in the history note. The lifecycle command prints the full approval rules:
  `toolkit work lifecycle`
- A question, a suggestion, a tentative answer ("probably B"), or silence is not an answer. Ask again in one line.
- An approval covers only what was shown. It never covers merge, deployment, spending, or publishing.
- A bare "yes", "ok", or "looks good" answers only a question asked earlier in this conversation. When none was asked, or the waiting question is not a yes-or-no question, show the decision with its choices and your recommendation, and record nothing.
- Set `waiting_on` to `agent` when the agent can continue, to `none` when nothing waits, or keep `owner` when another owner question is still open on that item.

## After a result approval

The item continues with `work-finish` (pull request, deployment, requirements baseline, Done). Open it when the owner wants it shipped now.

## Project-wide decisions

- A decision for the whole project goes in `DECISIONS.md`, not in memory and not in one item. Examples: "use Postgres everywhere", and a standing merge instruction ("agents may merge a pull request after an independent check finds no blocking issue").
- A decision that replaces an older one names it with `--replaces D-<n>`:
  `toolkit decision add --decision '<decision>' --why '<why>' --by <owner> --replaces D-<n>`
- A decision about one item stays in that item: its Recent History, the answered Open Questions row, and Notes > Decisions and context when the next session needs the context.
- `DECISIONS.md` is append-only. Never rewrite or remove a row; a changed decision is a new row that names the one it replaces.

## Tracker notes

- GitHub Issues or Jira: the `toolkit work` commands exit with code 3. Build the queue from the waiting-on-owner and stage 11 labels that `../../references/trackers/github.md` or `../../references/trackers/jira.md` names, and record answers as `../../references/trackers.md` says. Remove the waiting-on-owner label after each approval or last answer, as above.

# Work organize

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Shared rules: the work plugin's `references/conventions.md` and `references/trackers.md`, two folders above this skill's folder (`../../references/`). Cases and examples: this skill's `references/moves.md`. To open another skill, Claude Code uses the Skill tool; Codex reads that skill's `SKILL.md`. Run each `toolkit` command alone, on its own line, in both hosts: never joined by `&&`, `;`, or a pipe, and never from a script (in Codex that runs it inside the sandbox, where it fails). Text (conventions, "Text in a command"): one-line values (`--note`, `--effect`, `--append-row`, `--title`) go in single quotes, with an apostrophe written `'\''`, because double quotes run backticks and `$(...)`; section and design text goes on standard input in Claude Code (`<file>` is `-`, followed by a quoted heredoc, `<<'EOF'`), and in Codex in `--text '<text>'` or a file in a new `mktemp -d` folder, deleted right after the command. Never change a record with a script. Ask the owner in the reply text, never through a question tool. No remote (`git remote` prints nothing): never run `git fetch`, and never report a fetch refusal as a blocker.

## Steps

1. Rescan the tracker and read the tree. Read the report: moved, renamed, nested or un-nested, missing, duplicate id, record with no id, adopted copies of the template.
   `toolkit work sync`
   `toolkit work list --tree`
2. Say what the CLI already adapted (paths, a renamed folder, parent from location, Status from a dragged Notion Stage) in one line each ("WI-7 is now a sub-item of WI-3"), and what needs the owner's intent. The CLI already wrote a history row on each item the owner moved or renamed, and on the parents it left and joined; add a note only for his reason.
3. List side effects: a sub-item under a Done or Cancelled parent; a Roadmap phase listing a child that moved away; a `build` sub-item without approved requirements.
4. A missing item: ask whether it was removed on purpose (then cancel it with his words) or moved outside the tracker (ask where; move it back only after a yes). A copied folder with a duplicate id: the CLI renumbered the newer copy; confirm which one is the original.
   `toolkit work cancel <id> --reason '<his words>'`
5. Notion: a Stage the owner changed by dragging is kept. A card dragged to Done is not an approval: ask, and on a yes open `work-finish`.
6. Split (stage 05): propose the sub-items (title, what each delivers, which `R-xx` it covers), ask once, then create each one under the parent. A split never removes, renumbers, or rewrites the parent's `R-xx`: they stay in the parent, with their approval. A child that delivers approved parent requirements is made with `--covers`: it links them, copies no text, and inherits the parent's requirements approval, so the owner is never asked to approve the same requirement twice. A parent design the owner approved covers its children too: a `--covers` child of such a parent starts at planning (06), and its history row names that design; it gets no new design. Only a child that needs new behavior gets its own `R-xx` and its own approval. List the child ids in the parent's Roadmap Sub-items column. A child of an agent-led parent gets the same delivery value (`work-delegate` step 1). A split usually renames the parent: say the new title to the owner in one line before the title command below.
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 05-breakdown`
   `toolkit work set <id> --title '<new title>'`
   `toolkit work new --title '<title>' --type <type> --parent <id> --covers R-02,R-03`
   `toolkit work new --title '<title>' --type <type> --parent <id>`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section Roadmap --set-file <file>`
7. Nest, group, move, or archive on request. Before moving a folder, say how many nested items move with it.
   `toolkit work move <id> --under <parent-id>`
   `toolkit work move <id> --under <group>`
   `toolkit work move <id> --under archive`
   `toolkit work move <id> --under root`
8. Never move, regroup, cancel, archive, or restore on the agent's own initiative. Finish with validation and a short tree of what changed. `toolkit work move` writes the history rows on the item and on both parents; add a note only for the owner's reason. When a split or a move changed an item's next step, update the current focus (`../../references/conventions.md`, "The current focus"). End the reply with the one question for the owner, or the exact words that continue ("Say 'keep going' and I'll plan WI-008."), never with a plain statement of the next step.
   `toolkit work validate`
   `toolkit work history <id> --note 'Moved at the owner'\''s request: <his words>'`

## Rules

- A folder nested inside an item's folder is a sub-item; its parent follows its location. A plain folder with no record in it is a group and changes no parent. A sub-item cannot also sit in a group.
- `archive/` is a reserved group. Items there are hidden from the briefing and from the recommended next item. Archiving is not cancelling.
- Identity is the record's `id`, never the folder name. Renaming a folder or file keeps the item.
- Ids are never reused. When two records share an id, the one the CLI already knew keeps it and the newcomer gets the next free id.
- A record whose title is still `<Work item title>` is an unused template copy and is skipped.
- Never hand-edit `.work-items/DASHBOARD.md` or `.work-items/.toolkit-state.json`. The sync command in step 1 rebuilds them.
- Splitting keeps each child whole: its own roadmap and tasks, and its own result approval. Requirements and a design the owner already approved for the parent are linked and inherited, never copied or asked for again. Finishing a child never finishes or approves the parent.
- The owner's hand changes win. The CLI keeps them and reports them. Ask about a hand change only when it skipped a gate.

## Tracker notes

- Notion: nesting is the Parent item and Sub-items relation. Moving a card between groups on the board changes its Stage, not its parent.
- GitHub Issues or Jira: `toolkit work` exits with code 3. Use sub-issues or sub-tasks as `../../references/trackers.md` says. There is no folder layout to reconcile.

# Humanize Anything Sent to Another Person

Any text that will leave the project and be read by someone other than the owner
is run through the `humanizer` skill before the owner sees the final version.
Use the `unslop` skill when `humanizer` is not installed. That covers emails,
chat messages, support case text and comments, GitHub issues, pull request
descriptions, client documents, and any file made to hand to someone else.

Keep every fact, name, id, number, and date exactly as it was. Write it in the
owner's voice, first person, when it goes out under their name.

It does not apply to chat replies to the owner, work items, project knowledge,
code, or commit messages.
# Keep the Active Work Item Accurate

The work tracker is the source of truth for current work.

- Before substantial work, use the `work-on` skill. Read the active item's requirements, state, next step, and blockers.
- Save the owner's decisions, requirements, and corrections in the item or its linked document before moving on.
- When the work needs the owner's decision, add it to the item's Open Questions with "Decision needed from: owner" and set the item's `waiting_on` to `owner`. The `work-decide` skill records the answer.
- `build` and `data-load` work needs approved requirements before it starts. A later stage does not revoke that approval.
- After the owner accepts agent-led delivery, ask how the team is arranged. That choice authorizes helpers for that goal only.
- Mark an item Done only after the owner approves the result.
- Before ending unfinished work, record the exact next step in the item.

`toolkit work lifecycle` prints the stages, statuses, and approval gates. "Where information goes" in `AGENTS.md` is the routing table; the `work-delegate` skill holds the delivery offer and team questions, and the `handoff` skill holds the handoff steps.
# Review and Save Project Memory

This rule applies to the main agent. The project memory system is chosen at setup and recorded in `.toolkit.json`; with built-in memory it is the local `.memory/` folder. It is the single project memory store. Claude's native auto-memory and the `claude-toolkit` Second Brain plugin are disabled for this project. The session-start briefing shows the current focus in Claude Code and Codex. Do not treat a hook reminder as a save decision.

## Decide the destination first

Read the memory criteria (`.memory/memory-criteria.md` with built-in memory) and the likely owning record. Send current focuses, owner to-dos, and handoff context to the current focus; sourced terminology to the glossary; qualifying otherwise-unowned durable context to a topic; active work to the chosen tracker; decisions for the whole project to `DECISIONS.md`; accepted delivered behavior to requirements; the technical approach to the design kept with its work item; verified current structure to the System Guide; and repeatable procedure to instructions or a skill. Raw external documentation stays in its source folder. A small memory pointer can route future sessions to a hard-to-find authority without copying its body.

Review on explicit remember/forget requests, corrections, standing preferences, meaningful decisions or discoveries, significant fixes or episodes, people/tool/reference changes, focus shifts, work-item completion, and handoffs. The toolkit's `UserPromptSubmit` hook flags only explicit keep phrases, and its Stop hook checks once per turn that such a phrase was handled. Do not save on every hook reminder or every turn. A review can end with no memory.

## Approval

The `memory-save` skill holds the approval policy: what the owner's own words authorize, what needs a yes in onboarding mode, what trusted mode allows, and what always needs the owner. The mode is `memory.approval` in `.toolkit.json`; only an explicit owner instruction changes it. A yes authorizes the shown operation and meaning only. Silence does not. An unanswered save question is kept as a proposal: the agent does not rely on it, and `work-decide` shows it to the owner until he approves or rejects it. The `memory-save` skill says how.

If the owner says a proposed item should not be memory, withdraw it. Save only a general selection rule, as a `feedback` memory, if their feedback supplies one; do not restate the rejected fact in the current focus or another topic. Review similar candidates against that rule from then on.

## Saving and completion

The main agent saves memory itself through the `memory-save` skill, which runs `toolkit memory` commands; there is no curator agent. Search first with `toolkit memory find`, then save with `toolkit memory save`, retire with `toolkit memory retire`, and write the current focus or glossary with `toolkit memory focus --set-file` or `toolkit memory glossary --set-file`. The commands lock memory, refuse stale edits, and rebuild the index.

For a focus-only change or already-authorized glossary maintenance, save without a lasting-memory question. Several independent signals can be grouped into one save; do not run parallel writes against the same topic or index. Before claiming a save succeeded, read it back with `toolkit memory get` and run `toolkit doctor`; tell the user briefly what was retained or what needs a decision.
# Write Artifacts in Plain English

An artifact is something an agent generates for a person to look at: a
diagram, a chart, a dashboard, a visualization, a mockup, a slide deck, a
published page, or a generated document. This rule is about the words inside
one: the title, the headings, the labels, the notes, the captions, the body
text.

The project's output style says how the agent talks in chat. The words inside
an artifact follow the same style. This rule exists because the output style
reaches only the main chat: a helper agent, a skill, or a Codex session that
makes an artifact never sees it. Read the active style file when there is
one. Where this rule and that file differ, the style file wins.

## Write about the subject

Every word describes the thing the artifact shows. The reader opened it to
learn about that thing, not about the artifact or the conversation that
produced it.

- Do not narrate the artifact. "Here is where the change lands, but only the
  key pieces" says nothing about the system. Cut it, or say what changed.
- Do not tell the reader what matters. "Here is the load-bearing decision"
  tells them how to feel. Write the decision.
- Bring in the conversation only when it is the fact. A quote earns its place
  when the exact words are what the reader needs, and then it says who said
  it and when. A quote the reader cannot place is noise.

## A heading names what is under it

A heading is a label, not a hook. It says what the reader is about to look
at, in the words of the subject.

The four headings below are an example: a page of options for who can see and
edit which projects in a team web app. The left column sells the section; the
right column names it.

| Written | Say instead |
|---|---|
| Three ways to build the team tree, pick one | Team structure options |
| One question decides the whole shape | Decision: can a team lead edit their own team's projects? |
| Four facts that rule out the most obvious answers | How team access works |
| What shape actually hands to a real person | Project visibility by role |

A number belongs in a heading when the number is the fact: "Three departments
share one role". "Three ways to build it" only counts the section below, and
the reader can count.

## Use the real name

Call a thing what the system calls it, every time. In that example the real
names are team structure, project visibility, sharing rule, admin access, and
permission group. The page used picture words instead: "shape" for the team
structure, "lever" for a setting, "leaks" for access people should not have,
"flows up" for a manager getting access to their team's projects. That is
figurative language, and it is not allowed. It makes the reader translate, and
a reader who does not know the system cannot.

A term the reader may not know gets a plain definition the first time it
appears. After that, the term is used unchanged.

A box or label carries the real name. Anything it needs to say about itself
is one plain line.

## Say the plain thing

Use the active output style inside the artifact. This artifact rule also requires:

- Common words. Short sentences. One idea each.
- No figurative or metaphorical language. No idioms, no jokes, no picture word
  standing in for a real thing.
- No preamble. Start with the content.
- No closing line that sums up or cheers.
- Fewer words, never fewer facts. Every number, name, date, and quotation
  stays exactly as it is.

## What this rule does not decide

How the artifact is laid out: how many boxes, what an arrow says, where a
note goes, whether there is a key. Every artifact is different, and the agent
making it decides. This rule decides the words.
# Prepare a Session Handoff

When the owner says he is clearing context or ending the session, or asks for a handoff, use the `handoff` skill, whatever the session's length. When the session is long and the next step is complex, offer a handoff. Use the `handoff` skill. Before the handoff, review the current focus (`toolkit memory focus`) and the memory criteria; update the focus, and save only authorized lasting memory, with the `memory-save` skill. Then write the prompt. Skip the offer for small edits and quick lookups.
# Work Safely in a Shared Repository

Other sessions edit this repository now. Before your first edit, run:

```
git worktree list
git status
git fetch origin && git log --oneline -10
```

- An unknown worktree, moved branch, or change you did not make means other sessions are live. Do not fix it. Tell the owner.
- Code, rules, skills, hooks, settings: use your own worktree and branch (`git worktree add .claude/worktrees/<name> -b claude/<name>`). Exception: a one-file edit asked for directly.
- Documentation-only saves: open the `publish-docs` skill.
- In the shared primary checkout, never switch branches, reset, rebase, or stash.
- Never touch another session's branch or uncommitted work.
- Stage paths by name. Never `git add -A`, `git add .`, or `git commit -a`. Read the full staged diff.
- Never hand-edit a generated file.
- Before taking a sequential number, check every tracker folder, worktree, and the remote. On a later collision, renumber only your own.
- Land implementation by pull request, merged with the owner's approval. A standing merge instruction the owner gave for this project counts.
- Before a merge, compare `git diff --name-only <default-branch>...<branch>` with `git status` in the primary checkout. A file in both: stop, name it, ask the owner.
- After the merge, remove your worktree and branch.
# Local Work-Item Folders

This project tracks work in local folders under `.work-items/`. The folder is
Git-ignored, lives in the main checkout, and is shared by every worktree. It is
not backed up by Git: `toolkit export` is the backup.

## An item is found by its ID, not its path

- An item is a folder holding a record, `WORK-ITEM.md`, and `DESIGN.md` when a
  design exists. The frontmatter `id` (for example `WI-001`) is the item's
  identity. The folder name and the file name may change.
- Refer to items by ID everywhere. Find an item's files with
  `toolkit work show <id> --path`. Never guess a path.
- Create items only with `toolkit work new`. It takes the next ID under a lock,
  so parallel sessions never pick the same one. IDs are never reused.

## The owner may move folders, and the agent adapts

- The owner may move, rename, nest, or group item folders by hand. That is
  normal. `toolkit work sync` finds every item again by its ID; the session
  hooks and every `toolkit work` command run it. Report what moved and continue.
  Use the `work-organize` skill to reconcile anything the sync reports as
  missing or duplicated.
- A record inside another item's folder is that item's sub-item: its `parent`
  follows its location. A plain folder with no record is a group and changes no
  parent.
- `archive/` is a reserved group. Items there are hidden from the briefing and
  from `toolkit work next`.
- Never move, group, archive, or rename items on your own initiative. When the
  owner asks, use `toolkit work move <id> --under <id|group|archive|root>`.

## What the tracker ignores, and what it generates

- Ignored: `work-item-template/`, any folder whose name starts with `_` or `.`,
  and any record whose title is still `<Work item title>`.
- Generated by `toolkit work sync`: `DASHBOARD.md`. State kept by `toolkit work`:
  `.toolkit-state.json` (the ID-to-path map and the highest ID used). Never edit
  either by hand.
- Change frontmatter fields (stage, status, parent, waiting on, approvals) only
  with `toolkit work` commands. Body sections may be edited directly or with
  `toolkit work edit`; the hook checks the record after each edit.
- Keep any other files the owner put in an item folder.

# Work delegate

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Shared rules: the work plugin's `references/conventions.md` and `references/helpers.md`, two folders above this skill's folder (`../../references/`). Full method: this skill's `references/agent-led-delivery.md` and `references/team-arrangements.md`. To open another skill, Claude Code uses the Skill tool; Codex reads that skill's `SKILL.md`. Run each `toolkit` command alone, on its own line, in both hosts: never joined by `&&`, `;`, or a pipe, and never from a script (in Codex that runs it inside the sandbox, where it fails). Text (conventions, "Text in a command"): one-line values (`--note`, `--effect`, `--append-row`, `--title`) go in single quotes, with an apostrophe written `'\''`, because double quotes run backticks and `$(...)`; section and design text goes on standard input in Claude Code (`<file>` is `-`, followed by a quoted heredoc, `<<'EOF'`), and in Codex in `--text '<text>'` or a file in a new `mktemp -d` folder, deleted right after the command. Never change a record with a script. Ask the owner in the reply text, never through a question tool. No remote (`git remote` prints nothing): never run `git fetch`, and never report a fetch refusal as a blocker.

## Steps

1. This skill is the only place the delivery offer is made and recorded; other skills open it. Look for a delivery choice that covers this goal: the item's `delivery` value, its Notes > Decisions and context, and its parent's choice (a sub-item is part of its parent's goal and makes no offer: creating it with `--parent` already copies the parent's delivery value and says so; check it, and set it with a note naming the parent only when it is missing or differs). A quick question or small edit gets no offer. Neither does a small item (one or two tasks, no sub-items): record owner-led with the reason at once, so the offer stops appearing as an agent to-do, and go on.
   `toolkit work show <id> --section "Decisions and context"`
   `toolkit work set <id> --delivery owner-led --note 'Small item: one or two tasks, so no delivery offer.'`
   `toolkit work set <id> --delivery agent-led --note 'Part of <parent-id>, whose goal is agent-led.'`
2. No choice recorded: add the offer as an Open Questions row and set the item waiting on the owner, so the offer stays on the record if the session ends first; then ask exactly "Would you like agents to take responsibility for delivering this, with you acting as product owner?" in the reply text, as its last line, and wait for the answer before building. When he answers, here or when `work-decide` hands his answer over, the `--delivery` command in step 4 or 5 marks that row Answered and prints "Marked Q-xx Answered"; read that line instead of editing the row by hand. If the owner already said it in his own words ("you drive"), that is the answer; do not ask again.
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Open Questions" --append-row '| <next Q-id> | Would you like agents to take responsibility for delivering this, with you acting as product owner? | delivery | Open | owner |'`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on owner`
3. Yes: ask about the team. Where this chat can list, read, and message other chats (today, the Claude Code desktop app): "Do you want one team inside this chat, or do you want me to rename this chat to Main Orchestrator and coordinate other chats that each have their own team?" On any other host, say the multi-chat arrangement is not available here and ask: "Shall I run one team of helpers inside this chat?" After the Main Orchestrator choice only: "Do you want me to archive sessions after their task is fully complete, everything is merged and shipped, and you approved?"
4. Record the choice, the goal it covers, who said it, the date, the team arrangement, the archive answer, and the limits (delegation never includes merge, deployment, spending, or publishing beyond what was given) in Notes > Decisions and context. Set the delivery value, add one history note, and read it back.
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Decisions and context" --set-file <file>`
   `toolkit work set <id> --delivery agent-led`
   `toolkit work history <id> --note 'Agent-led delivery accepted by <owner>: <his words>'`
   `toolkit work show <id> --section "Decisions and context"`
5. No, or a later revoke: record it the same way; do not offer again for this goal unless it grows a lot or the owner asks.
   `toolkit work set <id> --delivery owner-led`
6. Run the team through the skill that handles each stage: the main agent plans, briefs `builder`, `researcher`, and `acceptance-checker` agents with their role files, gives one writer per path, and is the only writer of the work item.
   `toolkit work list --tree`
7. Stop at every owner gate: set the item waiting on the owner, ask the question through the skill that asks it (that skill sets it back to the agent after his answer), and keep working on anything the answer does not block.
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on owner`
8. Codex: this plugin's agents do not load there. Read the agent's file in this plugin's `agents/` folder and give its full text, with the brief, to a native Codex worker: the `spawn_agent` tool, started without this conversation (`fork_turns` set to `none`), so a checker never shares the builder's thread. With no worker, say no helpers ran and do the work directly.
9. Archive a chat only when its task is complete, merged and shipped, the report is saved, and the owner approved. Never delete a chat.
10. End every reply with the one question for the owner (the offer, the team question, or the next gate), or the exact words that continue ("Say 'go' and the team starts on P1.").

## What each answer allows

- **Accepted:** agents drive discovery, interviews, requirements, research, design, the authorized build, checks, and delivery for this goal, across sessions. The owner supplies product direction, settles tradeoffs, and approves results.
- **Team arrangement chosen:** authorizes focused, bounded helper agents for this goal only.
- **No to the team question:** no helpers; the main agent does the work itself.
- **Declined or revoked:** normal help and record upkeep continue. No offer again for this goal unless it grows a lot or the owner asks.
- Nothing here widens other limits: no merge, deployment, spending, or publishing beyond what was given. Existing approvals still count.

## Rules

- The choice belongs to the named goal. It does not carry over to another goal, a new item, or an unrelated sub-item.
- Missing tracker access is not a missing decision. Keep a choice you could not save in the handoff and save it when access returns.
- A failed save: lead with "Not saved". A write whose read-back failed: "Saved but not verified".
- A recorded lead or chat id is coordination information. It is not proof that an agent is still running.
- GitHub Issues or Jira: `toolkit work` exits with code 3. Record the choice in the issue body's Notes and a `delivery` label, as `../../references/trackers.md` says.

## Text in a command

The shell changes text before the command sees it. Inside double quotes it
runs anything between backticks and anything in `$(...)` as a command, and
puts that command's output in the text. The command then saves the text with
those parts missing and still prints "Saved". So:

- **One-line values** (`--note`, `--effect`, `--append-row`, `--title`,
  `--reason`, `--quote`, `--evidence`, `--description`, `--source`): put them
  in single quotes, in both hosts. Inside single quotes the shell changes
  nothing. Write an apostrophe inside them as `'\''`, for example
  `--note 'Owner'\''s words: "ship it"'`. Never use double quotes for text.
- **Section, design, focus, glossary, and memory text in Claude Code:** pass
  it on standard input with `--set-file -` (or `--body-file -` for a memory
  save) and a quoted heredoc. The quotes around `EOF` in `<<'EOF'` stop the
  shell from changing anything in the text, and no file is left anywhere. Claude Code
  refuses `rm` outside the project, so a temporary folder there could never be
  deleted. Write the command, then the text, then a line holding only `EOF`:

  ```text
  toolkit work edit <id> --section "<heading>" --set-file - <<'EOF'
  ```

- **The same text in Codex:** a heredoc runs the command inside the sandbox,
  so do not use one. Give short or medium text in single quotes
  (`--text '<text>'`; newlines inside the quotes are kept). For longer text,
  make a new folder for this one save with `mktemp -d` (its name is unique, so
  two sessions or two projects never share a file), write the file in it with
  the file edit tool (`apply_patch`), run the `toolkit` command alone with the
  file's full path, and delete the file and the folder right after the command
  succeeds (`rm <file>`, then `rmdir <folder>`), before you ask the owner
  anything. Never write the file and run the `toolkit` command in one shell
  command.

  ```text
  toolkit work edit <id> --section "<heading>" --text '<text>'
  toolkit work design <id> --text '<text>' --status proposed
  ```

- Never use a fixed name such as `/tmp/wi001-requirements.md`: every project
  starts at `WI-001`, so another session's save could land in this item.
- Never leave draft files inside `.work-items/`: a second `DESIGN.md`-shaped
  file there confuses the design lookup.

# WI-001: Add a --shout flag to the greet CLI — solution design

**Requirements:** WI-001  
**Design status:** Draft  
**Requirements checked:** `.work-items/WI-001-add-a-shout-flag-to-the-greet-cli/WORK-ITEM.md`, 2026-09-28  
**Last updated:** 2026-09-28  
**Design approval:** Pending

## What this design solves

People running `node bin/greet.mjs` can add `--shout` before or after an optional name and receive the entire greeting in capital letters. The command keeps its current greeting when the flag is absent. `README.md` will show how to use the flag. This design covers WI-001's agreed goal and no other flags.

## Requirements and design readiness

The approved requirements describe a complete result for this small command. Both requirements are Finalized, and neither needs another owner decision before design review.

| Requirement | Status in work item | Design coverage | Remaining decision or gap |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R-01 — Capitalize the whole greeting with `--shout` | Finalized, approved by Mike on 2026-09-28 | Option A: argument selection and uppercase output | None |
| R-02 — Document the flag | Finalized, approved by Mike on 2026-09-28 | Option A: `README.md` example | None |

## What exists today

Source inspection shows that `bin/greet.mjs` exports `greet(name = 'world')`, which returns `Hello, ${name}!`. Its CLI reads `process.argv.slice(2)` and passes only `args[0]` to `greet`. Thus the code currently treats `--shout` in the first position as a name. `test/greet.test.mjs` checks only `greet()` and `greet('Mike')`; it does not run the CLI. `README.md` shows the basic named greeting and no flag. These are code and file observations; the command has not been run for this design.

## Constraints and assumptions

| Type | Constraint or assumption | Source and status | Effect on the design |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Constraint | Keep the existing greeting when `--shout` is absent. | WI-001 R-01, approved 2026-09-28 | Leave the `greet` result unchanged unless the flag is present. |
| Constraint | `--shout` may precede or follow the optional name. | WI-001 R-01, approved 2026-09-28 | Select the name after excluding the recognized flag. |
| Constraint | Every CLI flag must be documented in `README.md`. | WI-001 R-02, approved 2026-09-28 | Add a description and working example for `--shout`. |
| Assumption | This change needs no dependency or new parser package. | Current `bin/greet.mjs` and `package.json`; proposed design choice | Use JavaScript array methods and `String.prototype.toUpperCase()` in the existing Node.js command. |

## Design options

### Option A — Extend the existing command

#### Approach

Change the CLI path in `bin/greet.mjs` to detect `--shout` and select the optional name from arguments other than that flag. Call the existing `greet` function, then uppercase its complete result only when `--shout` is present. Keep `greet(name = 'world')` and its exported behavior intact. Replacing the command or its `greet` function would require reimplementing behavior that already meets the no-flag requirement, with no benefit for this one flag and more risk of changing existing output. Add command-level tests with Node's built-in test tools and document the flag in `README.md`. This uses the current command and requires no dependency.

#### End-to-end behavior

1. A person runs `node bin/greet.mjs`, optionally with a name and `--shout` before or after that name.
2. The CLI checks whether the argument list contains `--shout`. It chooses the first argument other than `--shout` as the name, or uses the existing `world` default when no name remains. It builds the greeting with `greet` and applies uppercase to the whole greeting if the flag is present.
3. The command prints one greeting line. `--shout` alone prints `HELLO, WORLD!`; either `--shout Mike` or `Mike --shout` prints `HELLO, MIKE!`. Without the flag, no name prints `Hello, world!` and `Mike` prints `Hello, Mike!`.

#### Requirement coverage

| Requirement | Build or reuse | Why it meets the requirement | How to check it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R-01 | Change CLI argument handling and output in `bin/greet.mjs`; reuse `greet` and JavaScript `toUpperCase()` | Excluding the flag before choosing the name accepts both positions; uppercasing the completed greeting includes the name and punctuation stays in place; the no-flag branch keeps the current result. | Run command-level tests for `--shout`, `--shout Mike`, `Mike --shout`, no arguments, and `Mike` without the flag; run `npm test`. |
| R-02 | Change `README.md` | A flag description and executable command/output example show readers how to use it. | Review the README example and run its command to confirm the shown output. |

#### Technical shape

- **Components and files:** `bin/greet.mjs` is changed for CLI argument selection and conditional uppercase output. Its `greet` function is reused unchanged. `test/greet.test.mjs` is changed to add command-level tests using Node's built-in test and child-process tools. `README.md` is changed to document `--shout` with a working example. `package.json` and its `npm test` script are reused unchanged.
- **Data and state:** Arguments exist only for one process run. The command stores no data and needs no migration.
- **Access and security:** The local command has the same access as the user running it. No account, permission, or security rule changes.
- **Integrations:** The CLI receives process arguments and writes to standard output. The tests invoke the CLI as a child process. No external service is involved.
- **Operations:** Run `npm test` and the README example before delivery. A rollback restores the previous `bin/greet.mjs`, tests, and README. No monitoring or backup change is needed for this local command.

#### Tradeoffs and risks

| Tradeoff or risk | Likelihood and effect | Mitigation or owner decision |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Checking only the first argument would miss `Mike --shout` or greet the flag as a name. | Likely if argument selection is left as written today; R-01 would fail. | Search the full argument list for the flag and exclude it when choosing the name; test both positions. |
| Uppercasing only the fixed word `Hello` would leave a supplied name mixed case. | Possible; R-01 would fail. | Apply `toUpperCase()` to the complete greeting returned by `greet`; test `Mike` in both flag positions. |
| Changing `greet` itself could change imported calls without the flag. | Possible; existing behavior could regress. | Leave `greet` unchanged and test the CLI's no-flag output as well as its existing unit tests. |

1. Change `bin/greet.mjs` to identify `--shout`, select the optional name from the remaining arguments, and uppercase the final greeting conditionally. Depends on the approved R-01. Complete when the five specified CLI cases print their expected lines by direct command run.
2. Add command-level cases to `test/greet.test.mjs` for the three shouted inputs and two no-flag inputs. Depends on step 1. Complete when `npm test` passes and the tests would detect a wrong flag position or a mixed-case name.
3. Add the `--shout` description and a command/output example to `README.md`. Depends on step 1. Complete when the shown command prints the documented output and R-02 is covered.

toolkit memory: Save, find, and manage project memory: records, the current focus, and the glossary.

Usage:
  toolkit memory save --type <t> --name <slug> --description <d> (--body <text> | --body-file <file|->)
                      [--approved-by <who>] [--authorization <text>] [--supersedes <key>] [--source <text>]
                      [--status <s>] [--last-verified <YYYY-MM-DD|unknown>] [--expect <version|absent>]
                      [--proposal] [--allow-similar]
  toolkit memory find <query> [--reflect] [--type <t>] [--limit <n>] [--all] [--proposals]
  toolkit memory get <key>
  toolkit memory list [--type <t>] [--status <current|needs-review|retired|all>]
  toolkit memory approve <key> --by <name>
  toolkit memory reject <key> [--reason <text>]
  toolkit memory retire <key> [--superseded-by <key>] [--reason <text>]
  toolkit memory restore <key>
  toolkit memory rename <key> --to <new-key>
  toolkit memory delete <key> --owner-approved
  toolkit memory focus [--set-file <file|-> | --text <text>] [--expect <version>]
  toolkit memory glossary [--set-file <file|-> | --text <text>] [--expect <version>]
  toolkit memory reindex
  toolkit memory status
  toolkit memory export --to <folder>
  toolkit memory import --from <folder> [--dry-run]

Types: user, feedback, project, reference, event. A key is <type>_<slug>, for example feedback_deploy_window.
The key is also the file name without .md and the frontmatter name (the model's topic format).
A key typed with dashes (feedback_deploy-window) finds the same record.
A --name longer than 60 characters is refused, not shortened.
A body file that starts with frontmatter fills any field not given as a flag.
--approved-by writes "authorization: Approved by <who> on <date>". With no approver
and memory.approval trusted, it is "Trusted grant"; --authorization sets the words.
Saving over an existing record keeps its source, authorization, supersedes,
last_verified, and any other frontmatter fields unless they are given again.
Saving a record that needs review marks it verified today.
Duplicate check: save refuses (exit 2) and lists the records when memory
already has one with the same key, or one with a very similar description or
text. Update a record you read with --expect <version>, replace one with
--supersedes <key>, or save a different fact anyway with --allow-similar.
--proposal saves a record the owner has not answered yet ("Save to memory?"):
status needs-review, authorization "Proposed by the agent on <date>". A
proposal is not a fact: find leaves it out unless --proposals (or --all) is
given, and the briefing and toolkit work decisions list it for the owner.
approve records his yes (the record becomes current, "Approved by <name> on
<date>"); reject records his no and deletes the proposal. reject --reason
repeats his reason in the output; nothing keeps it, since the proposal is deleted.
delete, reject, retire, and rename also take the record out of the local
briefing cache (Hindsight and Notion memory) and the index.
toolkit memory focus keeps the "# Current focus" heading and the
"Last updated:" line, and adds them with today's date when they are missing.
A "Last updated:" date older than today is set to today: the save is today's update.
retire --superseded-by <key> marks the record superseded (the replacement must
exist and not be archived); retire alone archives it (built-in: moved to
.memory/archive/). A record saved with status superseded or archived keeps that
word; a superseded record stays beside the current ones.
Links to a note in other notes are repaired when it is renamed (rename, or save
--supersedes), superseded, archived (the link becomes its words plus "(archived)"),
or deleted (the link becomes its words); the notes changed are listed, and so
are notes whose links could not be repaired. Saving an archived note as current
moves it out of archive/ and keeps its links working.
